text: Lesson 29's cost-savings script only works if every VM is correctly tagged. Thornfield Analytics' finance team needs something broader: every resource in the subscription needs a CostCenter tag and an Owner tag, so spend can be charged back and someone is accountable for what exists. This lab builds that check in Python, pulling together Chapter 3's authentication pattern and Chapter 6's tag-compliance use case.

The core logic lists every resource in the subscription and checks its tags against a required list, collecting anything missing CostCenter or Owner into a violations list. Notice this script never changes anything — it only reads. A script that discovers a missing tag and silently guesses a value to fill it in would be worse than the problem it's solving, because nobody would know which tags were real and which were invented.

A list printed to a console disappears the moment the terminal closes, so the script writes its findings to a CSV file instead and exits with a non-zero status code if it found any violations. That exit code is the entire reason Chapter 7 matters here: a pipeline step doesn't read English output, it reads a number. Zero means success and the pipeline moves on; anything else means the step fails and surfaces as a check someone has to look at.

This script authenticates using DefaultAzureCredential from Chapter 3, which tries several credential sources automatically — a signed-in Azure CLI session on a laptop, or a pipeline's service principal once this script runs inside Chapter 7's CI/CD pipeline instead. Either way the script's own code never stores a secret, which is exactly why it can move from someone's laptop into a scheduled pipeline trigger with zero changes.

Scheduled nightly, the pipeline's own secret store supplies the credential, and the exit code decides every single night whether the subscription is in a clean state. The CSV file becomes a build artifact the pipeline keeps, so whoever responds to a failure has the exact list of offending resources in hand. Next up: a case study where a check exactly like this one caught a dangerous manual change before it caused real damage.
